gap_map.why_it_matters: dotnet-test covers execution and testability but not selection. The judgment about which behavior earns a test stays uncovered.
.NET solutions accumulate projects. Nothing decides when a folder should become a project, or when a shared project has turned into a grab bag that every other project references.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor applies references/growth-signals.md with the stack thresholds below.

layers.name: unit
layers.belongs_here: business rules in isolation, with fakes for infrastructure
layers.cost: fastest; Microsoft: if a behavior can be tested either way, choose the unit test
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test spins up WebApplicationFactory to check one calculation

layers.name: integration
layers.belongs_here: the real pipeline through WebApplicationFactory: routing, model binding, middleware, DI and the database
layers.cost: slower, more setup - and where middleware and DI defects actually surface
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the suite has an integration test per data permutation instead of a focused set

layers.name: e2e
layers.belongs_here: a browser driving the deployed app; Microsoft recommends Playwright for .NET for SPAs

testing.proportions: Microsoft: 'If a behavior can be tested using either a unit test or an integration test, choose the unit test.' And: do not write integration tests for every permutation of data and file access - a focused set of read, write, update and delete tests is usually enough.
rules: Keep unit and integration tests in separate projects. Microsoft recommends this so infrastructure components are not accidentally pulled into unit tests, and so you can run one set without the other.
Prefer the unit test when both would work. Reach for WebApplicationFactory when the pipeline itself is under test.
For EF Core in-memory testing, the SQLite provider is the recommended choice - the EF in-memory provider is for limited and basic testing only and does not enforce relational constraints.
A focused set of CRUD integration tests covers data access. Do not enumerate permutations there.
POST endpoints protected by antiforgery need the token and cookie retrieved from a prior GET - a test that skips this is testing the rejection, not the endpoint.
traps: The EF Core in-memory provider accepts writes a real database would reject, so the suite is green on data that cannot exist.
WebApplicationFactory resolves the real DI graph, so a test can pass because of a registration nobody intended to include.
Middleware ordering bugs are invisible to unit tests by construction - only the pipeline shows them.
Async void and un-awaited tasks in tests complete after the assertion, so the test passes before the work finished.
A shared WebApplicationFactory fixture carries database state between tests unless it is reset explicitly.
what_not_to_test: That the DI container resolves a registration, or that routing maps an attribute.
Auto-properties and records with no behaviour.
EF Core migration classes as units - run them.
Generated code and source generators' output.
testing.notes: WebApplicationFactory gives real integration tests over the actual pipeline, which catches the middleware and DI mistakes that unit tests structurally cannot see.

growth_thresholds.extract_service_layer: an endpoint or action method exceeds 30 lines
growth_thresholds.extract_project: >=2 projects reference the same internal folder by relative path

architecture.pattern: layered, with projects as the enforced boundary

layers.name: Endpoint / Controller
layers.holds: transport: routing, model binding, validation, response shaping
layers.must_not: hold business rules - an action past 30 lines has absorbed the service

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.holds: EF Core, external clients, file and queue access
layers.must_not: be referenced by the domain - the dependency points inward

layers.name: Domain
layers.holds: entities and rules with no framework dependency

variants.name: Single project, folders by feature
variants.cost: nothing stops a domain class from referencing EF Core

variants.name: Multiple projects per layer
variants.use_when: the boundary must be enforced by the compiler
variants.cost: more build and solution overhead; a project per layer with one class each is over-abstraction

rules: Dependencies point inward. Domain references nothing; infrastructure references domain, never the reverse.
A service never touches HttpContext. If it needs the caller, pass it as an argument.
Entities are not API responses. Return DTOs so a column rename is not a breaking API change.
A project boundary is the only boundary the compiler enforces. Folders are a convention and will be crossed.
Anything resolved from the DI container rather than constructed directly is invisible to the reference graph - list conditional registrations in CLAUDE.md.
architecture.notes: Microsoft publishes reference architectures rather than a single mandate. These rules are the common denominator across them plus the mentor's judgment - present them as such, not as doctrine.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Both are first-class and mixing them means two conventions for routing, filters and validation.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Two conventions means a cross-cutting concern gets implemented twice and forgotten once.

key_decisions.decision: Project layout: one project or many
key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Only a project reference is enforced by the compiler; folders are not.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Single project until a boundary is actually being violated.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Splitting late means untangling references that already point the wrong way; splitting early means solution overhead for nothing.

key_decisions.decision: Data access and the unit of work
key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: EF Core, Dapper and raw ADO.NET have very different transaction and tracking semantics.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: EF Core, with reads explicitly no-tracking.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Change tracking left on for read paths silently holds entities and turns a read endpoint into a memory problem under load.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: ASP.NET Core supports policy, role and claim-based authorization and enforces none by default.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Policy-based, with a default authorization policy so an endpoint must opt out rather than opt in.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Opt-in authorization means a forgotten attribute is a public endpoint that looks exactly like an intentional one.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Framework features available depend on where it runs.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Discovering at deploy time that the target does not support something you built on means rewriting those paths.

operability.observability: ILogger with structured logging, and OpenTelemetry for traces and metrics. Exception handling middleware is where an unhandled exception becomes a recorded, shaped problem response instead of a bare 500.
operability.authorization: Authorization policies. Set a default policy so endpoints must opt out with [AllowAnonymous] - then an unmarked endpoint is protected rather than public.
done_checks: the app starts with the production configuration
clean clone and build from scratch
rules: Register HttpClient through IHttpClientFactory with an explicit timeout. A raw HttpClient with the default timeout and no policy exhausts sockets and waits far too long.
Set a default authorization policy so a forgotten attribute fails closed instead of open.
Exception handling middleware reports unhandled exceptions. Without it they become 500s with no record.
Configuration is validated at startup with options validation, so a missing value fails the deploy rather than the first request.
EF Core migrations are applied deliberately, never automatically at startup in production - an automatic migration on a rolling deploy runs from several instances at once.

dead_code_risks: Types resolved from the DI container by interface rather than by direct construction
Controllers and endpoints reachable only through routing
Types instantiated by reflection, including serialization targets and source-generated code
EF Core migration classes discovered by assembly scan
public members of a class library consumed by another solution
Code behind a feature flag that is currently off
